clauses: The girl thus pointed out by the King was a daughter of one of the laborers employed by the royal gardener; and she had come to help her father weed the flower beds.
Now, Ernestine (for this was the name of the little girl) was fond of reading aloud, and often many of the neighbors would assemble at her father's house to hear her.
The King gave her the petition, and she rapidly glanced through the opening lines to get some idea of what it was about.
As she read, her eyes began to glisten, and her breast to heave.
"What is the matter?" asked the King; "don't you know how to read?"
"Oh, yes! sire," she replied, addressing him with the title usually applied to him: "I will now read it, if you please."
note: 'The girl'(c0)='Ernestine'(c1 named)='she' thereafter: naming-then-pronoun coref must be tracked to know who is being tested; role arc patient(described)->theme(named)->agent(reads)->experiencer->addressee->agent(replies).

clauses: "As for you, my young lady," continued the King, "I know you will ask no better reward for your trouble than the pleasure of carrying to this poor widow my order for her son's immediate discharge."
"Let me see whether you can write as well as you can read. Take this pen, and write as I dictate."
He then dictated an order, which Ernestine wrote, and he signed.
Calling one of his guards, he bade him go with the girl and see that the order was obeyed.
note: 'you/my young lady'(c0-1)='Ernestine'(c2)='the girl'(c3): same entity referenced by title, name, and description; role arc addressee->agent(writer)->theme(escorted).

clauses: How much happiness was Ernestine the means of bestowing through her good elocution, united to the happy circumstance that brought it to the knowledge of the King!
Then, there was the poor widow who sent the petition, and who not only regained her son, but received through Ernestine an order for him to paint the King's likeness.
so that the poor boy soon rose to great distinction, and had more orders than he could attend to.
And Ernestine had, moreover, the satisfaction of aiding her father to rise in the world, so that he became the King's chief gardener.
The King did not forget her, but had her well educated at his own expense.
note: Ernestine's role shifts across the passage from causal agent/instrument of others' good fortune (c0-1,3) to patient/beneficiary of the King's care (c4); requires tracking her cascading effects across 5 clauses.

clauses: And first, Charles Brown was sent into the room, and told that he would have to wait a little.
So Charles sat down on a chair near the door.
For some time he was very quiet, and looked about him; but there seemed to be so many curious things in the room that at last he got up to peep at them.
So he lifted up the cover.

This turned out to be a sad affair; for under the dish cover was a heap of very light feathers; part of the feathers, drawn up by a current of air, flew about the room, and Charles, in his fright, putting the cover down hastily, puffed the rest of them off the table.
the old gentleman... entered the room, to the consternation of Charles Brown, who was very soon dismissed as a boy who had not principle enough to resist even a slight temptation.
note: Single-entity 6-clause temptation arc: sent(patient)->waits(theme)->peeps(agent)->lifts cover(agent)->causes mess(agent)->dismissed(patient); clean role-variation case, no other named entity to confuse coref.

clauses: When the room was once more arranged, Henry Wilkins was placed there until such time as he should be sent for.
No sooner was he left to himself than his attention was attracted by a plate of fine, ripe cherries.
Taking fresh courage, he went cautiously and took a very fine cherry... and put it into his mouth.

Now, the old gentleman had placed a few artificial cherries at the top of the others, filled with Cayenne pepper; one of these Henry had unfortunately taken, and it made his mouth smart and burn most intolerably.
Henry Wilkins was sent about his business without delay, with his mouth almost as hot as if he had put a burning coal into it.
note: Henry: placed(patient)->tempted(experiencer)->takes cherry(agent)->suffers pepper-cherry(patient)->dismissed(patient); requires tracking that the 'artificial cherry' consequence in c3 depends on his own act in c2.

clauses: Rufus Wilson was next introduced into the room and left to himself; but he had not been there ten minutes before he began to move from one place to another.
Having looked around the room, he noticed a drawer to the table, and made up his mind to peep therein.
But no sooner did he lay hold of the drawer knob than he set a large bell ringing, which was concealed under the table.
Rufus was so startled by the sudden ringing of the bell, that all his impudence could not support him.

The old gentleman asked him if he had rung the bell because he wanted anything. Rufus was much confused and stammered, and tried to excuse himself, but it did not prevent him from being ordered off the premises.
note: Rufus causes his own trap (c2 agent) then becomes its startled experiencer (c3) then patient of dismissal (c4); the causal-then-experiencer flip on the SAME entity is the hard case.

clauses: George Jones was then shown into the room by an old steward; and being of a cautious disposition, he touched nothing, but only looked at the things about him.
At last he saw that a closet door was a little open, and he very cautiously opened it an inch farther.
He ventured to open the door another inch, and then another, till, the plug being pulled out of the barrel, the leaden shot began to pour out at a strange rate.
the shot falling upon this pan made such a clatter that George was frightened half out of his senses.
The old gentleman soon came into the room to inquire what was the matter, and there he found George nearly as pale as a sheet. George was soon dismissed.
note: George's own cautious opening (c1-2, agent) unintentionally triggers the shot-barrel consequence he then suffers (c3, experiencer); cross-clause causal chain over 5 clauses with a single tracked entity.

clauses: William Smith next entered the room, and being left alone soon began to amuse himself in looking at the curiosities around him.
William was not only curious and prying, but dishonest, too, and observing that the key was left in the drawer of a bookcase, he stepped on tiptoe in that direction.
The key had a wire fastened to it, which communicated with an electrical machine, and William received such a shock as he was not likely to forget.
No sooner did he sufficiently recover himself to walk, than he was told to leave the house, and let other people lock and unlock their own drawers.
note: William's dishonest intent (c1, agent stepping toward the drawer) is punished by the trap he does not foresee (c2, patient of shock); role flips from agent-of-attempted-theft to patient-of-consequence within one entity's span.

clauses: The other boy was Harry Gordon, and though he was left in the room full twenty minutes, he never during that time stirred from his chair.

Harry had eyes in his head as well as the others, but he had more integrity in his heart; neither the dish cover, the cherries, the drawer knob, the closet door, the round box, nor the key tempted him to rise from his feet.
the consequence was that, in half an hour after, he was engaged in the service of the old gentleman at Elm Tree Hall.
He followed his good old master to his grave, and received a large legacy for his upright conduct in his service.
note: Harry's role in c0 is agent-of-NOT-acting (negation-based agency, contrasted implicitly with the other boys); this restraint becomes the cause of his being hired (c2, patient/beneficiary) and later rewarded (c3, agent).

clauses: Conrad Lange, collector of the revenues of the city of Berlin, had long been known as a man whom nothing could divert from the paths of honesty.
On casting up his accounts at the close of a particular year, he found a deficit of ten thousand ducats.
Alarmed at this discovery, he went to the minister, presented his accounts, and informed him that he did not know how it had arisen, and that he had been robbed by some person bent on his ruin.

The minister received his accounts, but thinking it a duty to secure a person who might probably be a defaulter he caused him to be arrested, and put his accounts into the hands of one of his secretaries for inspection.
who returned them the day after with the information that the deficiency arose from a miscalculation; that in multiplying, Mr. Lange had said, once one is two, instead of once one is one.
note: Conrad Lange's role flips from known-honest theme (c0) to self-reporting agent (c2) to arrested patient (c3) purely via pronoun coref (no name repeated between c1-c3); the arrest is caused by his own honest self-report, an ironic dependency the reader must track.

clauses: The poor man was immediately released from confinement, his accounts returned, and the mistake pointed out.
During his imprisonment, which lasted two days, he had neither eaten, drunk, nor taken any repose; and when he appeared, his countenance was as pale as death.
On receiving his accounts, he was a long time silent; then suddenly awaking, as if from a trance, he repeated, "Once one is two."
While repeating his accustomed phrase, if anyone corrected him by saying, "Once one is one," his attention was arrested for a moment, and he said, "Ah, right, once one is one."
and then resuming his walk, he continued to repeat, "Once one is two." He died shortly after the traveler left Berlin.
note: Continues conrad_lange_accused: 'the poor man'(c0) is only resolvable as Conrad Lange via the PRIOR passage (cross-passage identity carry), then tracked purely by pronoun through his mental breakdown to death (c4); no name appears anywhere in this passage.

clauses: In the city of Bath, not many years since, lived a barber who made a practice of following his ordinary occupation on the Lord's day.

As he was on the way to his morning's employment, he happened to look into some place of worship just as the minister was giving out his text. He listened long enough to be convinced that he was constantly breaking the laws of God and man.
He became uneasy, and went with a heavy heart to his Sabbath task.
At length he took courage, and opened his mind to his minister, who advised him to give up Sabbath work, and worship God.
He discontinued his Sabbath work, went constantly and early to the public services of religion, and soon enjoyed that satisfaction of mind which is one of the rewards of doing our duty.
The consequences he foresaw actually followed. His genteel customers left him, and he was nicknamed "Puritan" or "Methodist."
He was obliged to give up his fashionable shop, and, in the course of years, became so reduced as to take a cellar under the old market house and shave the poorer people.
note: 7-clause single-entity arc (unnamed until a later passage): habitual-sin agent(c0)->convicted experiencer(c1-2)->reforming agent(c3-4)->socially punished patient(c5-6); requires holding the whole moral-cause chain to answer mid-passage role queries.

clauses: One Saturday evening, between light and dark, a stranger from one of the coaches, asking for a barber, was directed by the hostler to the cellar opposite.
Coming in hastily, he requested to be shaved quickly, while they changed horses, as he did not like to violate the Sabbath.
He burst into tears; asked the stranger to lend him a half-penny to buy a candle, as it was not light enough to shave him with safety.
When shaved, he said, "There must be something extraordinary in your history... Here is half a crown for you. What is your name?" "William Reed," said the astonished barber.
"Come along, follow me," said the stranger, "Your uncle is dead, and has left an immense fortune, which I will put you in possession of."

The stranger was soon legally satisfied of the barber's identity, and told him that he had great pleasure in transferring a great many thousand pounds to a worthy man, the rightful heir of the property.
note: Continuation of barber_reed_sabbath: the same reduced barber is sought out (theme), shaves the stranger (agent), breaks down in poverty (experiencer), is named and revealed as heir (patient/recipient); needs the earlier passage's poverty backstory to make sense of his tears in c2.

clauses: Turning aside, and passing through the ill-hung gate, I approached the dwelling. a slender girl, who had noticed my entrance, stood awaiting my arrival.

A deep, quick bark answered, and, sudden as an apparition, the form of an immense dog loomed in the doorway. At the instant when he was about to spring, a light hand was laid upon his shaggy neck, and a low word spoken.
"Go in, Tiger," said the girl, not in a voice of authority, yet in her gentle tones was the consciousness that she would be obeyed.
as she spoke, she lightly bore upon the animal with her hand, and he turned away and disappeared within the dwelling.
note: Tiger's role flips from threatening agent about to spring (c1) to obedient patient once commanded and touched by the girl (c2-3); the dog is unnamed until c2, so 'he'(c1)='Tiger'(c2) must be resolved retroactively.

clauses: "A stranger, mother," said the man who had given me so rude a greeting at the door; "and he wants us to let him stay all night."
The woman looked at me doubtingly for a few moments, and then replied coldly, "We don't keep a public house."

So unobtrusively that I scarce noticed the movement, the girl had drawn to her mother's side. What she said to her I did not hear; but I noticed, as she spoke, one small, fair hand rested on the woman's hand.
Was there magic in that touch? The woman's repulsive aspect changed into one of kindly welcome, and she said, "Yes, it's a long way to G--. I guess we can find a place for him."
note: The mother's state visibly changes across clauses (cold refusal c1 -> touched/receptive patient c2 -> warmly welcoming experiencer/agent c3), driven causally by the girl's quiet intervention in c2; requires linking cause (girl's touch) to effect (mother's changed reply) across clauses.

clauses: "Dick!" said the farmer in a peremptory voice, giving the rein a quick jerk as he spoke. But Dick moved not a step.
Next the whip was brought down upon him with an impatient hand; but the pony only reared up a little.
A stout lad now came out into the road, and, catching Dick by the bridle, jerked him forward; but Dick met this new ally with increased stubbornness.
The impatient boy now struck the pony on the side of the head with his clinched hand, and jerked cruelly at his bridle. It availed nothing; Dick was not to be wrought upon by any such arguments.
"Don't do so, John!" She was passing through the gate into the road, and in the next moment had taken hold of the lad and drawn him away from the animal.
And now that soft hand was laid gently on the pony's neck, and a single low word spoken. How instantly were the tense muscles relaxed.
The pony turned toward her, and rubbed his head against her arm for an instant or two; then he started off at a light, cheerful trot.
note: Dick's state carries and changes across 7 clauses: defiant refusing-agent (c0,2) under whip and jerking (patient, c1,3) -> calmed patient (c5) -> compliant agent (c6); John is a separate entity (the lad who is pulled away in c4) that must not be conflated with Dick.

clauses: This unfortunate individual was Samuel Duhobret, a disciple whom Durer had admitted into his school out of charity.
But he bore all with patience, and ate, without complaint, the scanty crusts given him every day for dinner, while his companions often fared sumptuously.
Meanwhile, the object of their mirth was tossing on a bed of sickness. Disease burned in every vein.
He awoke unrefreshed; it was the fifth day he had lain there neglected. He turned over, and feebly stretched out his hand toward the earthen pitcher: it was empty!
Samuel lay for a few moments thinking what he should do. He knew he must die of want if he remained there alone; but to whom could he apply for aid?
An idea seemed, at last, to strike him. He arose slowly, and with difficulty, from the bed, went to the other side of the room, and took up the picture he had painted last.
note: 'the object of their mirth'(c2) is an oblique re-description of Duhobret that must be coref'd back to the name; the arc runs patient-of-charity(c0)->long-suffering experiencer(c1-4)->decisive agent (c5), a clear turning point after 4 clauses of passivity.

clauses: He resolved to carry it to the shop of a salesman, and hoped to obtain for it sufficient to furnish him with the necessaries of life for a week longer.

Something whispered to the weary Duhobret, that here would be the market for his picture; he worked his way through the crowd, dragged himself up the steps, and, after many inquiries, found the auctioneer.
"What do you call your picture?" said the auctioneer, carefully looking at it. "It is a view of the Abbey of Newburg," replied the eager and trembling artist.
The auctioneer again scanned it contemptuously, and asked what it was worth. "Oh, that is what you please; whatever it will bring," answered Duhobret.
Poor Samuel sighed deeply. He nodded his head to the auctioneer, and retiring took his seat in a corner.
"Who bids at three thalers? Who bids?" was the cry. Duhobret listened eagerly, but none answered.
note: 'the eager and trembling artist'(c2) is a description-mention of Duhobret alongside name and pronoun mentions; his hope (c0-1, agent) sours into anxious silence (c5, experiencer) as the auction stalls, a state that only makes sense read across all 6 clauses.

clauses: "Mamma," said George West, as he came from school, "I can't help thinking about that poor little girl I told you of the other day. She looks so tired. I wish I could do something for her."
"Suppose you should carry her a handful of pretty flowers some time when you go to school," said Mrs. West. "I'll do that to-morrow morning," said George.
The next morning, as Jennie sat leaning her head wearily against the window, she spied George with a handful of beautiful flowers carefully picking his way across the street.
He stopped in front of her window, and, smiling very pleasantly, said, "How shall I find the way to your room?"

Jennie pointed to an alley near by, where he turned in, and found his way to the dingy staircase. Opening the door to Jennie's gentle "Come in," he said, "I have brought you a handful of flowers to look at this rainy day."
"Are they for me?" exclaimed Jennie, clapping her hands in delight. "How kind you are," she continued, as George laid them in her lap.
note: Jennie is introduced obliquely as 'that poor little girl'(c0) before being named in c2; her role shifts from talked-about patient to watching agent to receiving recipient, and George's plan in c1 must be linked to its execution in c4-5 across the passage.

clauses: "Did you use to live in the country?" asked George. "Oh, yes," answered Jennie, "we used to live in a beautiful cottage, and there were trees and flowers and green grass, and the air was so sweet."
"Well, what made you move here?" "Oh," said Jennie, softly, "papa died, and mamma was sick so long that the money was all gone."
"Then mamma had to sell the cottage, and she moved here to try to get work to do."
"Do you have to sit here all day?" asked George. "Yes," said Jennie, "because I am lame; but I would not care for that, if I could only help mamma."
"I declare, it's too bad!" said George. "Oh, no, it isn't," said Jennie, pleasantly; "mamma says maybe we should forget the Lord if we had everything we wanted, and He never forgets us, you know."
note: Jennie's lameness and confinement (c3) and calm faith (c4) only make sense as the DOWNSTREAM consequence of the father's death and poverty she recounts in c1-2; the causal backstory must be carried forward across all 5 clauses of first-person dialogue with no repeated name in some turns.

clauses: "Will you give my kite a lift?" said my little nephew to his sister. Lucy very kindly took it up and threw it into the air, but, her brother neglecting to run off at the same moment, the kite fell down again.
"now, how awkward you are!" said the little fellow.
Lucy once more took up the kite. But now John was in too great a hurry; he ran off so suddenly that he twitched the kite out of her hand, and it fell flat as before.
"Well, who is to blame now?" asked Lucy.
"I won't try any more," replied he, rather sullenly. "The kite won't fly, and I don't want to be plagued with it any longer."
And he did try, and succeeded, for the kite was carried upward on the breeze as lightly as a feather.
note: John is called 'my little nephew', 'her brother', 'the little fellow', 'John', and 'he' across clauses -- all one entity; his own carelessness causes the kite's failure in c0/c2 (he is the true cause, patient of the failure he made) yet he blames Lucy in c1, an irony requiring cross-clause tracking to catch.

clauses: There were, in very ancient times, two brothers, one of whom was rich, and the other poor. Christmas was approaching, so he went to his brother and asked him for a trifling gift.
The rich man was ill-natured, and when he heard his brother's request he took a fine ham down from the chimney, threw it at his brother, and bade him begone.
The poor man thanked his brother for the ham, put it under his arm, and went his way. He had to pass through a great forest on his way home.

"It is lucky for you," said the old man, "that you have met with me. If you will take that ham into the land of the dwarfs... you can make a capital bargain with it; demand for it the 'old hand mill which stands behind the door.'"
No sooner had he set his foot in it, than the dwarfs swarmed about him; but he refused all their tempting offers, and said that he would sell it only for the old hand mill behind the door.
So the bargain was made. The poor man took the old hand mill, and went back to the woods.
note: The poor man is humiliated and rebuffed by his rich brother (c1, patient) then becomes a resourceful bargainer with the dwarfs (c4-5, agent); the mill's significance in c5 depends on remembering the old man's instructions from c3.

clauses: "Where in the world have you been?" said his wife. "we have no wood to make a fire, nor anything to put into the porridge pot for our Christmas supper."
The house was dark and cold; but the poor man bade his wife wait and see what would happen. He placed the little hand mill on the table, and began to turn the crank.
First, out there came some grand, lighted wax candles, and a fire on the hearth, and a porridge pot boiling over it.
He was himself astonished at his good luck, as you may believe; and his wife was almost beside herself with joy and astonishment.
When the people went by the house to church, the next day, they could hardly believe their eyes. the poor man and his wife, dressed in nice new clothes, were seen devoutly kneeling in the church.
note: The poor man is scolded (c0, addressee), quietly acts (c1-2, agent), is astonished at the result (c3, experiencer), and finally is seen transformed in church (c4, theme) -- a full arc across 5 clauses continuing directly from fairy_mill_poor_brother.

clauses: At length, a great foreign merchant came, and when he had seen the mill, inquired whether it would grind salt.
The man would not sell it, of course; but every Christmas he ground out food and clothes and coal for the poor. So he rejected all the offers of the rich merchant.
The merchant, however, determined to have it; he bribed one of the man's servants to let him go into the castle at night, and he stole the mill and sailed away with it in triumph.
He had scarcely got out to sea, before he determined to set the mill to work. "Now, mill, grind salt," said he; "grind salt with all your might!"
The dishonest merchant was now very much frightened. The mill would not stop grinding; and at last the ship was overloaded, and down it went.
note: The merchant is rejected (c1, patient) then turns thief (c2, agent) then meets poetic-justice disaster (c4, patient again) -- a role round-trip across 5 clauses that also requires distinguishing 'the merchant' from 'the man'/mill_owner, a second tracked entity with overlapping pronouns.
